tools.name: get_catalog
tools.description:
List every macro series MacroRadar tracks and the model-output endpoints. Call this FIRST to pick a series, because picking one by name is guessing and this lets you pick by what it measures.

Each series carries a `concept` (what it measures: consumer-price-level, government-bond-yield, credit-spread, …), a `geography`, the `publisher`, `observation_start` (the earliest data that exists, which bounds any study over it), `discontinued` (the publisher's last observation, or null if the series is still live), `seasonality`, and `revisions`. The response also groups every series by concept up front, which answers "which series carry government bond yields, and for which countries" in one read. Each group is COUNTED as well as listed: `economies` is the distinct economies with a LIVE series, `scopes` holds `world` and bilateral pairs like `US/CA` separately, and `single_economy` marks a concept held for one economy only. Read those rather than counting the series list yourself — counted blind it is wrong three ways: a discontinued series looks live, four United States CPI variants look like four economies, and a currency pair looks like a country.

Why each of those decides something:
- `concept` — the compute grammar REFUSES to combine two levels of different concepts. INDPRO and PCEPI are both "Index 2017=100" and their difference is not a quantity. Checking concepts before composing an expression tells you what will be accepted.
- `seasonality` — three states, not two. "unadjusted" means a month-over-month change is dominated by the season and is refused; "not-applicable" is a market close, where mom is an ordinary question. Do not read FRED's two-state flag as this.
- `discontinued` — a series the publisher has wound down. Its history is real and a study over that history is a good question; what it cannot answer is "what is it now", and it must not be counted as current coverage. Nine series here were carried as if live, the oldest last observed in June 2021, and every other field agreed with the publisher.
- `revisions` — "published-once" means the publisher never restates a figure, which is exactly when an as-of question can be answered.
- `price_basis`, on ambiguous price series, says what the number IS and what it is not: MacroRadar's Brent is the EIA spot price, not the ICE front-month future.

tools.name: get_latest
tools.description: Latest value for one series with its current 10y/30y percentile and z-score. Accepts a FRED-style id (UNRATE) or a MacroRadar slug (unemployment-rate).

series.description: Series id or slug, e.g. UNRATE or unemployment-rate

tools.name: get_series
tools.description: Historical observations for one series (oldest first). Licensed series return metadata and a chart link instead of raw values. Use `limit` to bound the response and `derived` for per-date percentiles.

derived.description: Include 10y/30y percentiles and z-score per date

tools.name: get_regime
tools.description: MacroRadar's current macro regime read: growth, market, inflation, and financial-conditions classifications with probabilities, plus the fused composite score and 6-month recession probability. Historical indicator, not investment advice.

tools.name: get_regime_history
tools.description: Walk-forward history of MacroRadar's five-way regime probabilities (expansion, late cycle, slowdown, contraction, reflation) by month, each point from a model refit using only data available up to that date. Distinct from get_regime, which is the current cross-dimensional read (growth/market/inflation/financial-conditions) plus the fused composite score — this is that composite regime's own probability path over time. Historical indicator, not investment advice.

tools.name: get_recession_probability
tools.description: US 6-month recession probability from MacroRadar's walk-forward model — the latest reading, optionally with history.

tools.name: get_sentiment
tools.description: MacroRadar sentiment index (0-100 composite of seven market and survey components), optionally with its causal daily history since ~1990.

tools.name: get_whats_moving
tools.description: Every tracked indicator's latest move ranked by how statistically unusual it is against that series' own history, each with a checkable one-sentence summary. The place to start for 'what is happening in macro right now'.

tools.name: get_ranked
tools.description: Ranks a fixed list of major asset-class series (equities, Treasury yields, crude oil, the dollar index, VIX, credit spread) by how far their latest published observation sits from the midpoint of its own trailing 10-year percentile — largest distance first. A series needs at least 8 complete calendar years of span and at least 100 observations in that window to be ranked; short of either, it is excluded and the reason is stated. This is enumeration, not attribution: it says nothing about why a series is where it is. Licensed series (SP500, NASDAQCOM, VIXCLS, and others) return a `value_note` in place of the raw level while the derived percentile and side stay present; `recompute.licensed_series` names which ones — the same withholding rule get_whats_moving and run_study use. ?as_of and ?vintage are refused (400): the candidate series are read from a current-only projection and no archive of past rankings is held; per-series vintages are at get_series_as_of.

tools.name: get_breadth
tools.description: Counts, for every concept the registry tracks across more than one economy, how many of the observed economies sit in their own high or low tail together right now — the cross-country analogue of get_whats_moving, over economies rather than series. A concept only publishes as rankable breadth once at least `minimum_coverage` economies return a ranked reading (currently 4); short of that it reports `published: false` naming the count actually observed. Enumeration only: it counts which economies are in a tail, never why they got there. ?as_of and ?vintage are refused (400): the underlying selection is read from a current-only projection and no archive of past breadth snapshots is held; per-series vintages are at get_series_as_of.

tools.name: get_episodes
tools.description: Derived episode spans — curve inversions, volatility stress spells, bear markets, rate hiking/cutting cycles — including the OPEN spans ranked by how long they have run versus completed episodes of the same kind. Mechanical enumerations of the past, never a forecast.

series.description: Optional series id or slug to filter, e.g. T10Y2Y

tools.name: get_event_windows
tools.description: Decision-day windows: what each tracked market series did from the last close before an FOMC decision to the first close after it, with the latest decision's moves ranked within each series' own record.

series.description: Optional series id or slug to filter, e.g. DGS2

tools.name: get_calendar
tools.description: The consolidated macro schedule and recent record: US data releases, FOMC meetings and communications, ECB/BoE/BoJ rate decisions, and US trade actions, from the institutions' own published schedules. Pass from/to for an explicit historical range instead of the rolling window. Every event carries four timestamps — when it happened, when the source published it, when this record first held it, and when the record's copy was last revised.

from.description: Range start, YYYY-MM-DD. Requires `to`; max 1100 days.

tools.name: get_daily_log
tools.description: The macro record of one date (YYYY-MM-DD): tracked events, episode spans that opened or closed, FOMC decision-day moves ranked as of that date, and cited annotations. Also returns record_completeness — how many entries the record already held on the day itself versus picked up later, so a back-filled document is visible rather than silent. Episode and decision records reach decades back.

tools.name: get_policy_regimes
tools.description: US sanctions, tariff and export-control programmes as spans: how long each has been open, dated from a cited Federal Register instrument, with what the ingested record shows inside it. Durations are exact; action counts are bounded by the record start, which is returned alongside them.

tools.name: get_series_as_of
tools.description: What a series read on a PAST date, from the vintage archive — not what it reads now. Economic statistics are revised, so the CPI figure for June 2008 was one number on 15 September 2008 and is a different number today. Use this whenever the question is about what was known at the time: honest backtesting, 'what did the Fed see', or any claim dated to a moment. Answers distinguish three cases rather than collapsing to null: known_at (a real reading), not_yet_published (the number did not exist yet — a fact about the world), and no_archive (MacroRadar holds no vintage — a fact about MacroRadar). Pass `period` to also get the full revision history for one observation: what it first printed at, how many times it was republished, and where it stands now.

series.description: Series id or slug, e.g. CPIAUCSL

as_of.description: Read the archive as it stood on this ISO date, e.g. 2008-09-15

period.description: Optional. One observation period, e.g. 2008-06-01, to get its revision history as well.

tools.name: run_study
tools.description: Counts the past windows where the stated conditions held on a shared date, and reports the distribution of what followed at the stated horizon, plus the matched windows themselves and N — enumeration, not a forward-looking read. Each condition (threshold, percentile, or direction) and the measured expression are built from a series id, chained transforms (yoy, mom, diff, lag, annualized, zscore, percentile, movingAverage, index), and binary operators (plus, minus, times, over) chained left-associatively with no grouping — A minus B minus C means (A minus B) minus C, and a right operand is always a single series, never itself a binary expression — the same grammar `/compute` addresses. On a 422 refusal (too many conditions, an unbounded window, an unaddressable expression, and so on) the response's message is returned exactly as the API states it, never softened or retried. Raw values inside `windows` come back null for licensed (non-redistributable) series; `recompute.licensed_series` names which ones.

conditions.description: Every condition must hold on the same date for a window to match. 1-8 entries.

measure.description: The expression whose subsequent path is measured at each matched date.

horizon_periods.description: How many observations of measure's own spine ahead to measure the outcome.

dedupe_within.description: Matches within this many observations of each other count as one episode. Default 0 (no deduping).

tools.name: run_exposure
tools.description: Counts the past windows where the stated conditions held, and reports the distribution of a weighted basket's outcome over the stated horizon, plus the matched windows and N. Same condition grammar as run_study. `basket` holds up to 10 members (a bare series id and a weight, not an expression); the basket is rebalanced to those weights at the start of every matched window, and the outcome is the weighted sum of each member's own percent change to the horizon — no drift within a window, no compounding across them. On a 422 refusal the response's message is returned exactly as the API states it, never softened or retried. Raw per-member values inside `windows` come back null for licensed (non-redistributable) series; `recompute.licensed_series` names which ones.

basket.description: A long-only basket, 1-10 members, no duplicate series, all members the same observation frequency. Weights are FRACTIONS, not percentages — each strictly positive, and they must sum to exactly 1 within 1e-6 (0.6 and 0.4, never 60 and 40); a wrong sum is refused with the sum stated, never silently normalized.

series_id.description: A bare series id (not an expression) — the series held, not transformed.

weight.description: This member's fraction of the basket, strictly positive; all weights sum to 1.

conditions.description: Every condition must hold on the same date for a window to match. 1-8 entries.

horizon_periods.description: How many observations ahead, on the basket's own spine, to measure the outcome.

dedupe_within.description: Matches within this many observations of each other count as one episode. Default 0 (no deduping).

tools.name: get_studies
tools.description: Conditional history: every past window where stated macro conditions held together, and what followed each one. Call with no arguments to list the published studies; call with `study` for one study's full result. Use this when asked what happens next — the honest answer is a count, and this returns one: N matching windows, every date, the distribution of what followed, and how many are still running. It deliberately contains NO probability, expected value or forecast, because none of those are recomputable from the record. Each window carries a log_url for the day it began, and `recompute` says whether the inputs can be refetched from this API or must come from FRED (some series are display-only).

study.description: Study slug, e.g. inverted-curve-unemployment. Omit to list all.

tools.name: compute
tools.description:
Compute any expression the MacroRadar grammar can express, and get back the numbers WITH the plan that produced them. Expressions look like FEDFUNDS (a series), CPIAUCSL.yoy (year-over-year), CPILFESL.yoy.zscore_120 (chained, applied left to right), or FEDFUNDS~minus~CPIAUCSL.yoy (the real policy rate). Transforms: yoy, mom, diff_N, lag_N, annualized_N, zscore_N, percentile_N, movingAverage_N, index_YYYY-MM-DD. Operators between two expressions: plus, minus, times, over.

Prefer this over fetching series and doing the arithmetic yourself. Macro arithmetic has failure modes that are invisible in the output — percent-changing a series already quoted in percent, differencing two index levels with different bases, mixing frequencies without an alignment rule — and this refuses each of them with a named reason instead of returning a plausible wrong number. A rate is differenced into percentage points; a level is divided into a percent change; yoy is a calendar span, so it means the same thing on a daily series as on a monthly one.

A refusal is an answer, and the `refusals` field says exactly what would have been wrong.

`as_of` is answered only when EVERY input series is one the publisher never restates — eleven of ours, each a daily market close, where what was knowable on a date and what the record says now are the same numbers. For anything that gets revised it is refused, naming which input caused it, because the vintage archive is not backfilled and answering from today's figures would be wrong in precisely the way a point-in-time question exists to avoid. Check `revisions` in get_catalog to know which is which before asking, or use get_series_as_of for per-series reads over the archive itself.

This computes and describes. It does not say what happens next — for what followed the last N times a condition held, use get_studies.

expr.description: The expression, e.g. FEDFUNDS~minus~CPIAUCSL.yoy. Needs no URL encoding.

from.description: Optional ISO date; drop observations before it.

to.description: Optional ISO date; drop observations after it.

as_of.description: Optional ISO date. Answered only when every input is a series the publisher never restates (revisions: published-once in get_catalog); refused otherwise, naming the input that gets revised.

tools.name: get_claims
tools.description: MacroRadar's claims ledger: every kind of quantitative sentence the site renders, with the exact rule that produces it and the steps to recompute it from public data. Use this to verify or cite any MacroRadar figure.
